This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed investing to full-service wealth management all in one place, no matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Ronan. Attorney General Todd Blanche is defending a Justice Department lawsuit. It seeks to block Alaska from automatically certifying its U.S. Senate results.
If a Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses in next week's vote because there's another candidate on the ballot with the same name, Willem Marx reports the top Democrat in Alaska in the Senate race is joining others, asking a judge to reject that lawsuit.
The suit argues that a second candidate on the ballot, a retired schoolteacher named Daniel J. Sullivan, could confuse voters in the incumbent's tight race against Democrat candidate Mary Peltola.
Asked on CNN's State of the Union whether the lawsuit was setting the stage for President Trump to challenge the results, Blanche said his department was not, quote, "laying any groundwork" for the president to do that.
The relief that we are seeking is not to not certify. It's to not certify if the law is broken. So if the law is broken, and that's for Alaskan and the Alaskan court system to determine.
Alaska's courts had already ruled the second Sullivan could remain on the ballot, and state officials had listed the Senator as "Dan S. Sullivan" with his party label and incumbent status to help tell the two men apart.
For NPR News, I'm Willem Marx.
Serbia's long-serving leader has conceded defeat in a staff parliamentary election this month of after student-led protests against corruption in demands for political change.
The results mark a political earthquake with record numbers voting. Guy Delaunay reports from Belgrade.
Thousands of mostly young people are gathering at one of the busiest crossroads in the center of Belgrade, and they're all here celebrating because Alexander Vucic, the long-time populist leader of Serbia, has conceded defeat in the parliamentary elections.
He's admitted that his Serbian Progressive Party hasn't gotten nearly so many votes as the student list.
That's a group of candidates put together by Serbia's young people who've been protesting against Mr. Vucic, who they say is corrupt.
For NPR News, I'm Guy Delaunay in Belgrade, Serbia.
The Federal Reserve meets this week to decide whether or not to raise interest rates. NPR's Stephen Bshaha reports it'll be the last time for the Fed to get together before the election.
President Trump selected Kevin Walsh to chair the Federal Reserve earlier this year, with Trump clear that he wants interest rates to go down.
Instead, the Fed raised rates in September for the first time in more than three years to tamp down inflation.
Since then, inflation has remained hotter than expected. The Labor Department reported consumer prices were up 3.7% in September from a year earlier.
Investors still mostly expect the Fed will hold rates steady this month, but economists also see a December rate hike as more than likely.
Stephen Bshaha, NPR News.
And from Washington, this is NPR News.
A 76-foot-tall Engelmann spruce tree was harvested yesterday in Idaho. It was selected as this year's capital Christmas tree to be displayed on the west lawn of the U.S. Capitol.
Lorne Patterson was there when the tree began to get cut down.
Around 60 people gathered in a muddy gravel lot across from the towering evergreen to watch it come down.
Government officials gave remarks, and Nez Perce tribal members were present for speeches and ceremonies.
Well, if we think about it, we're actually taking a life.
That's Shannon Wheeler, the Nez Perce tribal chaplain.
We hope that the understanding of it actually being taken from its home and giving to the nation and to the world means something far greater.
After a drum circle and tribal blessing, the tree was chainsawed at the base.
It will be making stops in several western and midwestern states before its final destination.
For NPR News, I'm Lauren Patterson in Weipe, Idaho.
Officials in Ukraine say they are disputing.
Elon Musk's claim that Ukraine's military violated the terms of the Starlink satellite Internet system.
Using it, he said, for offensive military uses.
A Ukrainian defense official says the Starlink restrictions are making it impossible for the military to use.
Earlier this month, Ukraine drones lost Internet connectivity, disrupting the country's air defenses,
and Musk later acknowledged that he throttled down the Starlink system, saying it is not to be used for non-offensive purposes.
I'm Dan Roman, NPR News, Washington.
